content.value:
Subsystems don't normally have access to telemetry — only the OpMode does. To debug a subsystem, you'd pass references around or expose getters.

OpModeManager solves this with static access to the active telemetry, hardware map, and OpMode — from anywhere.

OpModeManager.getTelemetry() — the active telemetry object. Call telemetry.addData() from inside a subsystem.

OpModeManager.getActiveOpMode() — the current OpMode.

OpModeManager.getHardwareMap() — the active hardware map.

OpModeManager.getRobotState() — INIT, RUNNING, or STOPPED.

BuggySubsystem has a MotorEx and a simple proportional controller. Each tick, error = targetPower - currentPower, then currentPower += error * 0.02.

This is a geometric decay — it approaches the target but never quite reaches it. Without a deadband, the motor is forever inching toward the target.

steps.title: Surface debug values from the subsystem

content.value: In periodic(), after runControl(), use OpModeManager.getTelemetry() to output internal state. No references needed — the subsystem accesses telemetry on its own.

Before OpModeManager: to see subsystem state, the OpMode would need getters and manual telemetry wiring for every subsystem.

After OpModeManager: each subsystem writes its own debug telemetry. Adding a new subsystem doesn't touch existing debugging code.

Start the OpMode and watch Buggy/currentPower converge to targetPower, with the deadband snapping it to the target once error drops below 0.01.

content.question: Why use OpModeManager.getTelemetry() instead of passing telemetry into the constructor?
options: Every subsystem gets telemetry without manual wiring — cleaner as the robot grows

content.question: What was the root cause of the motor never reaching its target before the fix?
options: Geometric decay — error halves each tick but never reaches zero without a deadband
